title: How Wildfires Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how wildfires work, opening with the 2002 Rodeo-Chediski fire in Arizona, started by a Bureau of Indian Affairs firefighter (Leonard Greg) and collided with a fire set by a stranded woman. They cover the fire triangle (fuel, oxygen, heat), flash point, US wildfire statistics, human causes and lightning, the fuel, weather and topography factors, fuel load and moisture, wind as an oxygen delivery system, fire-created weather such as fire whirls and crown fires, spotting, and dry hot conditions. They discuss prescribed burns and their benefits, post-fire mud slides (Storm King Mountain, Colorado), firefighting methods like hotshots, smoke jumpers, backfire fire breaks, and aerial retardant, and debunk a scuba-diver-in-a-tree urban legend. Includes tangents on the movie Firestorm, Always, and a listener-mail-free closing with calls to action.

segments.title: Opening banter and Rodeo-Chediski fire story
segments.summary: Josh opens with banter and recounts the 2002 Rodeo-Chediski fire in Arizona, started by Leonard Greg, a Bureau of Indian Affairs firefighter, and collided with a fire set by a stranded woman; the fire burned about 467,000 acres and Greg was convicted of arson.

segments.title: The fire triangle and flash point
segments.summary: Chuck explains the fire triangle of fuel, oxygen and heat, and the flash point concept, including the flash point of wood and books.

segments.title: Wildfire statistics and causes
segments.summary: The hosts cite US wildfire statistics, including about 96,000 wildfires in 2006 with roughly four-fifths human-caused, and discuss lightning season, fire weather, and FEMA figures on intentional outdoor fires.

segments.title: Fuel, weather and topography
segments.summary: The three main factors controlling wildfire behavior are fuel, weather and topography. Fuel load, moisture, twig and pine straw density, and flashy fuels are discussed.

segments.title: Wind, fire-created weather and fire whirls
segments.summary: Wind acts as an oxygen delivery system and pushes fire. Dr Terry Clark's coupled fire atmospheric model is described. Fire whirls, crown fires, hairpin vortices, spotting, and the role of temperature and time of day are covered.

segments.title: Camping fire restrictions and personal anecdotes
segments.summary: Chuck shares his experience with campfire restrictions in western states and admits to a campfire on the Grand Canyon rim, saying it was irresponsible.

segments.title: Topography, slope and post-fire mudslides
segments.summary: Fires typically burn uphill and steep slopes speed them up. Burned roots lead to erosion and mudslides, including the Storm King Mountain fire near Glenwood Springs, Colorado, after which heavy rain buried part of Interstate 70 and the Guatemala slide is mentioned.

segments.title: Prescribed burns and their benefits
segments.summary: Prescribed burns clear underbrush, reduce accidental fires, release nutrients, and reduce disease. North America was managed with burns before Columbus.

segments.title: Firefighting: hotshots, smoke jumpers, fire retardant
segments.summary: Hotshot crews build firebreaks and backfires, smoke jumpers parachute in, and air tankers drop fire retardant, which contains phosphate fertilizer. The scuba-diver-in-a-tree urban legend is debunked.

segments.title: Movie tangents, listener mail note and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film Firestorm, mention Always, note there is no listener mail this week, and give calls to action for reviews, Twitter, Facebook, email, and the HowStuffWorks wildfire article.
